title: What Is the Best Plant Disease Identification App, and Is There a Free One?
metaTitle: Plant Disease Identification App: Accuracy and Free Options
metaDescription: A plant disease identification app is a first opinion, not a verdict. See what field tests found, what to look for, the free options and how to confirm.
excerpt: The best plant disease identification app covers your crop, reads the photo with the crop's age and weather, and tells you how to confirm. No app is right every time. In a field test, PlantVillage Nuru named cassava disease symptoms correctly 65 percent of the time, and 74 to 88 percent when it read six leaves per plant. For a free first guess, Plantix says its photo diagnosis is free. anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, has a Disease Finder and Pest Finder, and Anee, its smart farm technician, reads your photo with your season's records.

blocks.text: Search for an app to identify plant disease and you get hundreds. A 2022 review in the journal Agronomy found 606 plant disease detection apps in three app stores and kept 17 that fit its criteria. Most scored well on looks and ease of use, but poorly on the AI that reads the leaf. So the real question is which app helps you reach the right answer before you spend on a spray.

items: No app is right every time, and mild, early signs fool apps most.
Send several photos. Six leaves per plant gave the Nuru app its best results.
Pick an app that covers your crop, asks its age and place, and tells you how to confirm.

Free options: Plantix says its photo diagnosis is free, and a DA crop protection center in Caraga lists lab diagnosis as free. In anee.io, the [Disease Finder and Pest Finder](/features/pest-and-disease-finders) sort the signs by crop.
Confirm with a field check, a technician or a lab before you spray.

blocks.text: Photo apps and hotlines you may already know

Whatever the store calls it, a plant disease identifier app or a plant disease ID app, the idea is the same: a model that learned from photos of sick leaves. Plantix, for example, says on its own site that you take a photo of your sick crop and get a free diagnosis and treatment suggestions. In the 2022 review, it was the only app that could identify plants from images, detect diseases and suggest treatments. PlantVillage Nuru gives its diagnosis and advice even offline.

For rice, see our guide to [crop disease diagnosis apps](/blog/crop-disease-diagnosis-app). To ask a person, text the PhilRice Text Center at 0917 111 7423, or see how to [ask an agriculturist online](/blog/ask-an-agriculturist-online).
How accurate is a plant disease identification app?

A 2020 study in Frontiers in Plant Science tested PlantVillage Nuru on cassava farms in Tanzania and Kenya. Nuru named the symptoms of cassava diseases correctly 65 percent of the time. That beat the extension agents, at 40 to 58 percent, and the farmers, at 18 to 31 percent.

Two findings matter for every grower. First, one leaf is not enough. When Nuru read six leaves per plant, three upper and three lower, its accuracy rose to 74 to 88 percent. Second, early signs are hard. On leaves with mild symptoms, Nuru was right only 13 to 37 percent of the time.
Why a photo can fool the app

items: **Mild signs.** The first spots are faint, just when you most want an answer.
**Look alikes.** The Nuru study warns that some symptoms can pass for mineral deficiency.
**Unknown crops.** An app names only what it learned, so check its crop list.
**Hidden infections.** Some virus infections show few or no symptoms, the study notes.

blocks.text: So treat every diagnosis from a plant app as a first opinion. Our page on [AI farm advice](/blog/ai-farm-advice-accuracy) explains how to check one.

blocks.text: Is there a free plant disease identification app?

Yes, and a free plant disease app is a good first stop. Plantix says on its own site that its photo diagnosis is free. Use a free app for a fast first guess, then check it against a second source.

For that second look, the [Disease Finder](/features/pest-and-disease-finders) inside anee.io asks your crop and what you see, from spots and wilting to rot and mottled leaves. Then it names the diseases that fit, what to do first and the active ingredients with their FRAC groups, or why no spray helps. The Pest Finder does the same for pests, and the Weed Control Helper covers weeds. You open them from the tools in anee.io, and [pricing](/pricing) shows which plans include them.

blocks.text: How does anee.io read a photo of a sick plant?

A finder sorts the signs, while Anee, the [smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) inside anee.io, goes one step further. Send her a photo in Tagalog, Bisaya, Ilocano, Taglish or English. First, she reads the lot, its growth stage, the weather and what you already applied. Then she tells you what it most likely is and what to check next.
Where Anee stops

items: Anee needs internet and uses credits, on Libre plus Anee and the paid plans.
She cannot run a lab test, so for a suspected virus she tells you how to confirm it.
The free Libre plan has no chat, shows a few ads and holds one active season.

blocks.text: How do you confirm before you spray?

items.title: Photograph more than one leaf
items.text: Take three upper and three lower leaves, then the whole plant and the patch around it.

items.title: Compare two answers
items.text: Run the Disease Finder, then compare its list with a photo app or with Anee.

items.title: Do the field check
items.text: Look for ooze, mold, insects at the base or rot in the stem. Our guide to telling a [pest or disease](/blog/pest-or-disease-how-to-tell) apart shows how.

items.title: Send a sample when in doubt
items.text: The DA's Regional Crop Protection Center in Caraga lists plant disease diagnosis as free. You bring a fresh sample, and the lab work takes about four days. Ask your municipal agriculturist which center serves you.

items.title: Decide, then record
items.text: Pick a product registered with the FPA for your crop and follow its label. Then save the photos as a note.

blocks.title: Do not spray on a guess
blocks.text: An app that is right 65 percent of the time is wrong about one time in three. Also, no fungicide stops a virus. So confirm first, then follow the product label and its FPA registration.
Questions about plant disease identification apps

items.q: Can an app identify plant disease from one photo?
items.a: Sometimes, when the signs are clear. Still, in the Nuru study, reading six leaves per plant raised the app's accuracy to 74 to 88 percent. So send several photos.

items.q: What is the best free plant disease identification app?
items.a: The best free one covers your crop and tells you how to confirm. Plantix describes its photo diagnosis as free. Then compare its answer with a second source, such as the anee.io Disease Finder or your municipal agriculturist.

items.q: Is there a free tree disease identification app?
items.a: Check the crop list first, since a photo app names only what it learned. In anee.io, the Disease Finder covers farm trees such as mango, banana, coconut, cacao, coffee and durian. Our guide to [plant disease detection for fruit growers](/blog/plant-disease-detection-for-fruit-growers) covers more.

items.q: Do plant disease apps work offline?
items.a: Some do, such as Nuru. In anee.io, Anee needs a signal, but your notes and photos keep working offline and sync later.

items.q: Which plant disease app tells me what to spray?
items.a: The anee.io finders name active ingredients with their groups, never brands, or say when no spray helps. For the rate, follow the product label.
